translations.text: To strengthen your faith, we wish to tell you of the Saviour's birth according to the order of the Gospel:
how on this present day he was born in true humanity, [?] in divinity.
Luke the Evangelist wrote in Christ's book that at that time the Roman emperor Octavian issued a decree that the whole world should be registered in writing.
This registration was carried out by Cyrenius, the governor of the land of Syria, so that every man everywhere had to declare his lineage and his property in the city to which he belonged.
Then Joseph, Christ's foster-father, went from the land of Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, to a city of Judea which was David's,
and was called Bethlehem, because he was of David's kindred, and he wished to declare, together with Mary, her lineage; she was then still with child.
Then it happened, while they were staying in the city of Bethlehem, that her time was fulfilled when she was to give birth, and she then gave birth to her firstborn son,
and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid the child in their asses' manger, because there was no room in the inn.
There were shepherds in that region keeping watch over their flock; and behold, God's angel stood beside them, and God's brightness shone around them, and they were greatly afraid.
Then God's angel said to the shepherds, "Do not be afraid; behold, I announce to you great joy, which will come to all people;
for today the Saviour Christ is born to you in the city of David. You will see this sign: you will find the child wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger."
Then suddenly, after the angel's speech, a great multitude of the heavenly host was seen, praising God and singing, "Gloria in excelsis Deo,
et in terra pax hominibus bone uoluntatis," that is in our language, "Glory be to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men who are of good will."
And then the angels departed from their sight to heaven. Then the shepherds said among themselves, "Let us go to Bethlehem and see this word that God has shown us."
Then they came quickly and found Mary and Joseph, and the child laid in a manger, just as the angel had told them.
Then the shepherds truly understood the word that had been told them about the child, and all who heard it marvelled, and also at what the shepherds told them.
Mary truly kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.
Then the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, just as had been told them by the angel.
My dearest brothers, our Saviour, the Son of God, co-eternal with and equal to his Father, who was always with him without beginning,
deigned that on this present day, for the redemption of the world, he would be born in the body of the virgin Mary.
he is the Prince and Creator of all goodness and peace, and he sent before his birth an unusual peace, for never before that time was there such peace on earth
as there was at the time of his birth, so that the whole world was subject to the rule of one man, and all mankind paid royal tribute to him alone.
Truly, in such great peace was Christ born, who is our peace, because through his incarnation he joined angels and men into one household.

He was born in the days of the emperor who was called Octavian, who enlarged the Roman empire so greatly that the whole world submitted to him; and for that reason he was called Augustus, that is, 'increasing his realm.'

That name befits the heavenly King, Christ, who was born in his time, who increased his heavenly kingdom and with human nature filled up again the loss that the falling devil had caused in the host of angels.
Not only did he simply make up the loss, but he also greatly increased it.
Truly, as great a number of mankind comes through Christ's incarnation to the hosts of angels as there remained of holy angels in heaven after the devil's fall.

The emperor's decree, which ordered the whole world to be registered, clearly signified the deed of the heavenly King, who came into the world in order to gather his chosen ones from all nations and write their names in eternal blessedness.

This registration was carried out by the governor Cyrinus [Quirinius]. Cyrinus is interpreted as 'Heir', and he signified Christ, who is the true heir of the eternal Father; and he grants us to be heirs with him and sharers of his glory.
Then all the peoples went, so that each should register individually, in the city to which he belonged.
Just as at that time, by the emperor's decree, every single person declared himself in his own city, so too now teachers make Christ's decree known to us,
that we should gather ourselves into his holy church, and in it pay him the tribute of our faith with a devout mind, so that our names may be written in the book of life with his chosen ones.

The Lord was born in the city that is called Bethlehem, because it had been prophesied beforehand in these words: "You, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means the least of cities among the rulers of Judah;
for truly out of you shall come the leader who shall rule the people of Israel." Christ chose to be born on a journey, so that he would be hidden from his persecutors.

Bethlehem is interpreted as 'House of Bread', and in it Christ, the true bread, was born, who said of himself, "I am the living bread that came down from heaven, and whoever eats of this bread shall not die for ever."
We taste this bread when we go to the Eucharist with faith, because the holy Eucharist is spiritually Christ's body, and through it we are redeemed from eternal death.
Mary then gave birth to her firstborn son on this present day, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and for lack of room laid him in a manger.
That child was not called her firstborn child because she bore another afterwards, but because Christ is the firstborn of many spiritual brothers.
All Christian people are his spiritual brothers, and he is the firstborn in grace, and in divinity the only-begotten of the Almighty Father.
He was wrapped in poor swaddling clothes so that he might give us the immortal tunic that we lost through the transgression of the first-created man.
The Almighty Son of God, whom the heavens could not contain, was laid in a narrow manger so that he might free us from the confinement of hell.
Mary was a stranger there, as the gospel tells us, and because of the crowding of the people the inn was very cramped.
The Son of God was cramped in his lodging so that he might give us a spacious dwelling in the kingdom of heaven, if we obey his will.
He asks nothing of us in return for his toil except the salvation of our souls: that we prepare ourselves for him clean and unstained, for bliss and eternal joy.
The shepherds who kept watch over their flock at Christ's birth signified the holy teachers in God's church, who are the spiritual shepherds of faithful souls;
and the angel announced Christ's birth to shepherds because to the spiritual shepherds, that is, the teachers, the truth about Christ's humanity is most fully revealed, through the teaching of books;
and they must diligently preach to those placed under them what has been revealed to them, just as the shepherds spread abroad the heavenly vision.
It is fitting for the teacher always to be watchful over God's flock, so that the invisible wolf does not scatter God's sheep.
Angels were often shown to men under the old law, but it is not written that they came with light; rather, that honour was kept for the glory of this day,
that they revealed themselves with heavenly light, when the true light sprang up in the darkness for the right-minded: the merciful and righteous Lord.
The angel said to the shepherds, "Do not be afraid; behold, I proclaim to you great joy, which shall come to all people, for today the Saviour Christ is born in the city of David."
Truly he proclaimed great joy, which shall never end; for Christ's birth gladdened the inhabitants of heaven, the inhabitants of earth, and the inhabitants of hell.
The angel said, "Today the Saviour Christ is born to you in the city of David."
Rightly he said "day" and not "night", for Christ is the true day, who by his coming drove away all the ignorance of the old night and lit up the whole world with his grace.
The sign that the angel told the shepherds we should always keep in our memory,
and to thank the Saviour that he deigned to become a sharer in our mortality, clothed in human flesh and wrapped in poor swaddling clothes.
Then suddenly, after the angel's speech, a great multitude of the heavenly host was seen, praising God and singing, "Glory be to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men who are of good will."

One angel announced to the shepherds the birth of the heavenly King, and then suddenly many thousands of angels appeared, lest the authority of a single angel should seem too slight for so great a proclamation;

and all of them together sang out God's glory in joyful song and proclaimed peace to good men, clearly showing that through his birth men would be turned to the peace of one faith and to the glory of divine praise.
They sang, "Glory be to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men who are of good will." These words show that God's peace dwells where there is good will.
Indeed, mankind was at discord with the angels before the Lord's birth, for through sins we were estranged from God; therefore we were also reckoned as estranged from his angels.
But after the heavenly King took on our earthly body, his angels turned to peace with us; and those whom they previously despised as weak, they now honour as their companions.
Truly, in the old law, Lot and Joshua and every other who saw angels bowed down toward them and worshipped them, and the angels permitted it;
but John the Evangelist, in the New Testament, wished to worship the angel who spoke to him, and the angel forbade him that,
and said, "See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant, and the fellow servant of your brothers; worship God alone."
Before the Lord's coming, angels allowed human beings to fall down before them, but after his coming they refused this,

because they saw that their Creator had taken on the nature that they had formerly considered lowly, and they did not dare to despise it in us, since they worship it above themselves in the heavenly King.
Nor do they scorn the fellowship of men, when they fall down and pray to the God who became man.
Now we are counted as citizens of God, and like the angels; let us therefore take care that sins do not separate us from this great honour.
Truly, men are called gods; therefore, O man, guard your divine dignity against sins, for God has become man for your sake.
Then, after the angels' departure, the shepherds said among themselves, "Let us go to Bethlehem and see the word that has come to pass, which God has revealed to us."
Oh, how rightly they confessed the holy faith with these words: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God"!
A word is a manifestation of wisdom, and the Word, which is the Wisdom, is begotten of the Almighty Father without beginning; for he was always God from God, Wisdom from the wise Father.
He is not made, for he is God and not a creature; but the Almighty Father created all creatures through the Wisdom, and gave life to them all through the Holy Spirit.
Our human nature could not see Christ in his divine birth; but that same Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, so that we might see him.
The Word was not changed into flesh, but it was clothed with human flesh.
Just as each man exists in soul and in body as one man, so too Christ exists in divinity and humanity, one Christ in one person.
They said, "Let us go and see the word that has come to pass," because they could not see it before it was made flesh and became man.
Yet the divinity is not mingled with the humanity, nor is there any separation between them.
We could give you a small example, if it were not too lowly: look now at an egg, how the white is not mixed with the yolk,
and yet it is one egg. Likewise Christ's divinity is not blended into his humanity, but he nevertheless remains for ever in eternity in one person, undivided.
Then the shepherds came quickly and found Mary and Joseph, and the child laid in the manger. By God's ordinance Mary was betrothed to the righteous Joseph, for her great protection;
because it was the custom among the Jewish people, according to the law of Moses, that if any woman had a child other than in lawful marriage, she was to be stoned to death.
But God sent his angel to Joseph when Mary was with child, and commanded him to take care of her and to be the child's foster-father.
It seemed to the Jews as if Joseph were the child's father, but he was not; for the Almighty Creator had no need to be born of a woman;
rather, he took his humanity from Mary's womb, and left her a virgin, not defiled but made holy through his birth.
She never had intercourse with a man, she gave birth without pain, and she remains a virgin. The shepherds saw, and understood what had been told them about the child.

There is no blessedness without the knowledge of God, just as Christ himself said when he commended us to his Father: "This is eternal life, that they know you, the true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ."
And all who heard it were greatly amazed at it, and at what the shepherds said.
Mary truly kept all these words, pondering them in her heart. She would not make Christ's secret widely known, but waited until he himself revealed it when he wished.
She knew God's law, and had read in the writings of the prophets that a virgin was to bear God. Then she rejoiced greatly that she was allowed to be that virgin.
It had been prophesied that he would be born in the town of Bethlehem, and she marvelled greatly that she had given birth there, in accordance with the prophecy.
She remembered what a certain prophet had said: "The ox knew its lord, and the ass its lord's manger." Then she saw the child lying in the manger, where the ox and the ass usually look for food.
God's archangel Gabriel had announced to Mary the coming of the Saviour into her womb, and she saw then that his message had been truly fulfilled. Mary kept such words, pondering them in her heart.
And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, just as it had been told to them.
The memorial of these three shepherds is kept one mile east of Bethlehem, displayed in a church of God to those who visit the place.
We should imitate these shepherds, and glorify and praise our Lord for all the things that he did for love of us,
for our redemption and for eternal bliss. To him be glory and praise with the Almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.
